title: 1976-09-15_Dorothy_199.txt
concise_summary: PKD argues that 'Thomas'—an immortal apostolic Christian from Acts A.D. 45—is his 'master' or authentic self latent in his psyche, while PKD the writer is merely a mask or phenomenal appearance. The world of Acts is not historically past but immanent and overlaid with 1974 America via a 'push-pull' system where observer and observed cannot be separated. This explains his 27-year obsession with identical themes, his 1970 breakthrough in The Tears of Sophia, the 2-3-74 visions, and Nixon's overthrow as a covert divine irruption by secret apostolic Christians.
key_claims: Thomas is an absolute, immortal personality—the 'master self'—while PKD is a relative, phenomenal mask. When the mask-ego collapses under stress, Thomas is revealed.
Rome A.D. 45 (the world of Acts) is not relegated to the past but exists as immanent reality, locked in a two-mirror ('Magdeburg hemispheres') system with USA 1974.
The 1970 writing, 1974 anamnesis, and 3-74 visions erupted not from PKD but from Thomas acting through him; Thomas is the source, not the product.
The Tears of Sophia depicts not a fictional future world with Acts material inserted, but rather reveals that the modern world is latently the world of Acts itself—the mirror reality.
Nixon's overthrow was a 'raid' by Christ/God using secret immortal apostolic Christians latent in some people, culminating in a theophany visible only to those hosts and to PKD through Thomas.

Reality comes in two orders: the noumenal (Dinge-an-Sich, Acts, absolute, actual) versus the phenomenal (Maya, Dokos, USA 1974, seeming). What is real is the mystical corpus Christi replacing the universe of blind determinism.

tensions: How can Thomas be 'here' in PKD's head yet 'locked into Rome A.D. 45'? PKD resolves this by denying Rome is in the past—it is immanent—but the paradox remains: what does 'immanent' mean across a 1900-year temporal gap?

If both Romans and Americans were seen as 'syntonically blending' (not competing), were they truly separate realities or aspects of one? PKD affirms Acts is 'absolute' but struggles with the logic of superimposition.
PKD claims he must not reveal Thomas's existence due to a 'stricture of silence,' yet publishes extensive analysis in the Exegesis. Is the silence itself part of the protection?
The novel The Tears of Sophia predates PKD's conscious realization of Thomas, yet PKD reads it retrospectively as encoded revelation. How much is discovery vs. hermeneutical projection?
PKD asserts Nixon's overthrow is 'not subjective but objectively true,' yet grounds it in the 'secret immortal xtians' no one else perceived. How does this escape solipsism?
Is Thomas truly a distinct personality or an alter-ego/archetype?  PKD emphasizes the distinction but also describes Thomas as always knowing PKD, suggesting interpenetration rather than division.

This superimposition could syntonically blend. This is crucial. They did not compete, as I said supra, I saw people as simultaneously romans + americans, inhabitants of CAD 45 + AD 1974.

Beyond any doubt I experienced a theophany, + very likely recaptured the lost oral Gnosis of apostolic times. I was in apostolic times! + it in me. The irruption of Acts + Thomas is a subjective apocalypsis for me—but...in my view reality is subjective—in the mind—only.
uncertainty_flags: Father Rasch is mentioned as connected to The Tears of Sophia but is not otherwise identified; unclear if this is the author PKD knew or a fictional character.
Will McNally and his article on MITHC (possibly Lies Incorporated?) is cited but not fully contextualized in the surviving Exegesis.
The 'stricture of silence' preventing PKD from publishing about 'immortal authentic apostolic Xtians' is asserted but not explained. Is this self-imposed or external?
PKD twice notes he should 'avoid solipsism' via the volvox push-pull system, but the mechanism is unclear: how does intersubjective reality emerge from purely subjective mental orders?
The identity of 'Kathy' in the Canadian dream is ambiguous—possibly his ex-wife Kathy Tyne, but unconfirmed in this passage.

PKD states about The Tears of Sophia: 'I was not familiar with Acts, which I was not when I (sic) wrote it'—the sic suggests uncertainty about whether he had read Acts before writing, undermining the claim of Thomas's authorship.
